steps.title: Divisibility signs & remainders
steps.intro: Know when a number divides — without dividing.

tables.title: Divisibility signs
head: Divisible by
Check
Example
rows: last two digits are divisible by \(4\)
last three digits are divisible by \(8\)
split into parts with no common factor: \(3\cdot4\), \(3\cdot5\), \(2\cdot9\), \(3\cdot8\)
NOT \(12=2\cdot6\): \(6\) is divisible by \(2\) and by \(6\), but not by \(12\)

tables.title: Remainders
head: Fact
Example
rows: Remainder \(r\) when dividing by \(d\): \(N = dk + r\)
By \(3\) or \(9\): same remainder as the digit sum
Sum, product: add or multiply the remainders
Difference: subtract; if negative, add the divisor
\(a\) and \(a+b\) are divisible by \(d\) → \(b\) is divisible by \(d\)
New divisor that divides the old one: keep the remainder (divide it again if too big)
leaves \(13\) by \(15\) → leaves \(3\) by \(5\); by \(8\) → by \(6\): unknown

tables.title: Divisibility stories
head: Situation
Method
Example
rows: build from the inside and multiply the denominators

tips: "What could the number be?" → eliminate what it can't be.
"Which expression could be the number?" → plugging in \(x = 0\) is safe and fast (each choice keeps its remainder).
"Necessarily divisible by?" → never plug in a value that gives \(0\): zero is divisible by everything.

steps.stem: In Daniel's class, \(\frac{1}{5}\) of the students are boys who play basketball, and among those, \(\frac{1}{3}\) also play the guitar. What could be the number of students in the class?
explanation: A fifth of the class are basketball boys, so the class is divisible by 5. A third of the basketball boys play the guitar, so the basketball group is divisible by 3.
Build it from the inside: guitar players \(k\), basketball boys \(3k\), the class \(5\cdot3k=15k\). The class is divisible by 15.
Only \(45=15\cdot3\) works: \(45\div5=9\) and \(9\div3=3\) ✓.
\(35\div5=7\), but 7 is not divisible by 3. 42 and 32 are not divisible by 5.

steps.stem: Tamar is putting her stamps into an album. If she arranges them in rows of 5 with an equal number in each row, 4 stamps are left over. If she arranges them in rows of 3 with an equal number in each row, 1 stamp is left over. What could be the number of stamps Tamar has?
explanation: We need a number that leaves remainder 4 when divided by 5 and remainder 1 when divided by 3. Test the choices.
\(28=5\cdot5+3\): remainder 3, not 4 ✗. \(40=5\cdot8\): remainder 0 ✗.
\(34=5\cdot6+4\) ✓ and \(34=3\cdot11+1\) ✓. Both conditions hold.

steps.stem: \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers. \(x\) is the remainder when \(a\) is divided by 8, and \(y\) is the remainder when \(b\) is divided by 3. What is the greatest possible value of \(x\cdot y\)?
explanation: The biggest remainder is one less than the divisor: \(x\le8-1=7\) and \(y\le3-1=2\).
Both are possible, for example \(a=7\) and \(b=2\). So the greatest value is \(7\cdot2=14\).
24 is the trap: \(8\cdot3\). A remainder is always smaller than the divisor.

steps.stem: A number leaves a remainder of 4 when divided by 5. Which of the following expressions could represent the number (\(x\) is an integer)?
explanation: A multiple of 5 plus a number: only that number decides the remainder.
(1) \(5x+7=5(x+1)+2\), so the remainder is 2 ✗.
(3) \(10x+8=5(2x+1)+3\), so the remainder is 3 ✗.
(4) \((5x+5)^2=25(x+1)^2\), so the remainder is 0 ✗.
Faster: plug in \(x=0\): \(7\), \(4\), \(8\), \(25\) leave \(2\), \(4\), \(3\), \(0\). Here \(x=0\) is safe, because each expression leaves the same remainder for every \(x\).

steps.stem: \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers, and \(a>b\). When \(a\) is divided by 7, the remainder is 2. When \(b\) is divided by 7, the remainder is 5. What will be the remainder if \(a-b\) is divided by 7?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
explanation: Subtract the remainders: \(2-5=-3\).
A remainder cannot be negative, so add the divisor: \(-3+7=4\).
Trap: \(5-2=3\) subtracts in the wrong order.

steps.title: More remainder tools
steps.intro: The tools of the advanced questions, each with one example.

tables.title: Tools
head: Situation
Method
Example
rows: write the first and last as \(d\cdot k\); count \(=\) last \(k-\) first \(k+1\)
multiply or add only the units digits; powers repeat
two → divisible by \(2\); three → divisible by \(6\)

Tag it: write each condition as \(d\cdot k\). Multiply → tags multiply; add → only the shared factor; divide → every factor of the bottom must be in the tags; "by \(a\) and by \(b\)" → the LCM. \(k\), \(m\) guarantee nothing.

tips: Plugging in: one value that fails knocks out a choice. Values that work prove nothing — keep going until one choice is left.
Never plug in a value that gives \(0\) in a "necessarily divisible" question.
The smallest case gives the biggest POSSIBLE divisor, not the answer: \(A(A+4)(A+20)\) with \(A=2\) gives \(264\), but only \(24\) is certain.

steps.stem: \(30\%\) of the members of a sports club play tennis. Which of the following numbers could be the number of members who play tennis?
explanation: \(30\%=\frac{30}{100}=\frac{3}{10}\). Build it from the inside: the club has \(10k\) members, and \(3k\) of them play tennis.
So the number of tennis players is divisible by 3. Digit sums: \(530\to8\) ✗, \(540\to9\) ✓, \(550\to10\) ✗, \(560\to11\) ✗.
Only 540 (for example, a club of 1,800 members).
12 tokens means the number is divisible by 2 and by 3.
By 3: the digit sum \(6+1+X=7+X\) is divisible by 3, so \(X=2\), \(5\) or \(8\).
By 2: \(X\) is even, so \(X=2\) or \(X=8\) (612 and 618). Two values.

steps.stem: Which of the following numbers is not divisible by 12?
explanation: \(12=3\cdot4\), and 3 and 4 have no common factor. So check 4 (last two digits) and 3 (digit sum). Not \(2\cdot6\): 6 is divisible by 2 and by 6, but not by 12.
Last two digits: 28, 52, 72 and 16 are all divisible by 4.
Only \(3{,}152\) is not divisible by 3, so it is not divisible by 12.

steps.stem:
Yoav claims: "There are more three-digit numbers divisible by both 3 and 5 than three-digit numbers divisible by 17."
Michal claims: "There are more three-digit numbers divisible by both 3 and 7 than three-digit numbers divisible by both 2 and 13."
Which of the following is correct?
explanation: Count the multiples: write the first and the last as \(d\cdot k\), then count \(=\) last \(k-\) first \(k+1\).
By 3 and 5, that is by 15: from \(105=15\cdot7\) to \(990=15\cdot66\), so \(66-7+1=60\) numbers. By 17: from \(102=17\cdot6\) to \(986=17\cdot58\), so \(58-6+1=53\). Since \(60>53\), Yoav is right.

By 3 and 7, that is by 21: from \(105=21\cdot5\) to \(987=21\cdot47\), so \(47-5+1=43\). By 2 and 13, that is by 26: from \(104=26\cdot4\) to \(988=26\cdot38\), so \(38-4+1=35\). Since \(43>35\), Michal is right too.
Both are right.

steps.stem:
Given:
\(\begin{cases} c=4a \\ a=\frac{b}{5} \end{cases}\)
\(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are positive integers. Which claim is not necessarily true?
explanation: Write everything with \(a\): \(b=5a\) and \(c=4a\).
\(c=4a\) is divisible by 4 ✓. \(b=5a\) is divisible by 5 ✓. \(a+b+c=a+5a+4a=10a\) is divisible by 10 ✓.
\(a+b=6a\). For \(a=1\): \(a+b=6\), which is not divisible by 12. So claim (3) is not necessarily true.

steps.stem:
\(x\) and \(y\) are positive integers. \(x\) is divisible by \(6\), and \(y\) is divisible by \(9\).
What is the largest number that \(x+y\) is necessarily divisible by?
explanation: Tag each condition: \(x=6k\) and \(y=9m\), where \(k\) and \(m\) are unknown positive integers.
Add: \(x+y=6k+9m=3(2k+3m)\). Only the shared factor \(3\) comes out. \(2k+3m\) is unknown, so it guarantees nothing more.
So \(x+y\) is always divisible by \(3\). Nothing bigger is certain: \(x=6\), \(y=9\) gives \(15\) (not divisible by \(9\) or \(18\)), and \(x=12\), \(y=9\) gives \(21\) (not divisible by \(15\)).
Trap: \(x=y=18\) gives \(36\), which is divisible by \(18\) and by \(9\). Different letters need different values.

steps.stem: Given: \(x=5a^3-5a\) (\(a\) is a positive integer). \(x\) is necessarily divisible by:
explanation: \((a-1)a(a+1)\) is three numbers in a row, so it is divisible by 6. Therefore \(x\) is divisible by \(5\cdot6=30\).
Check with \(a=2\): \(x=5\cdot8-5\cdot2=30\). It is not divisible by 60, 40 or 20, so only 30 is certain.

steps.stem: Given: \(x=14a+6\) (\(a\) is a positive integer), and \(x\) is divisible by 10. Which of the following could be the value of \(a\)?
explanation: \(x\) is divisible by 10, so \(x\) ends in 0. Since \(x=14a+6\), \(14a\) ends in 4.
The units digit of \(14a\) depends only on \(4\cdot\)(the units digit of \(a\)): \(4\cdot3=12\), \(4\cdot4=16\), \(4\cdot5=20\), \(4\cdot6=24\) ✓.

steps.stem: Yael loaded 900 points onto an amusement-park card. The first ride cost \(x\) points, the second ride cost \(2x\) points, and the third ride cost \(3x\) points. Which of the following could be the number of points left on her card after the three rides?
explanation: She paid \(x+2x+3x=6x\) points, so the number of points she paid is divisible by 6 (by 2 and by 3).
For each choice, find what she paid: \(900-15=885\) (digit sum 21, but odd ✗), \(900-24=876\) (even ✓, digit sum 21 ✓), \(900-26=874\) (digit sum 19 ✗), \(900-32=868\) (digit sum 22 ✗).
So 24 points are left, and \(x=876\div6=146\).

steps.stem:
When \(x\) is divided by 8, the remainder is 4.
Yuval claims: "\(2x\) is necessarily divisible by 8."
Noga claims: "\(x\) is necessarily divisible by 4."
Itay claims: "\(x\) is necessarily divisible by 12."
Which of the following is correct?
explanation: Write \(x=8k+4\).
Yuval: \(2x=16k+8=8(2k+1)\) is divisible by 8 ✓.
Noga: \(x=8k+4=4(2k+1)\) is divisible by 4 ✓. (4 divides 8, so a remainder by 8 also gives the remainder by 4.)
Itay: \(k=0\) gives \(x=4\), which is not divisible by 12 ✗. (12 does not divide 8, so a remainder by 8 says nothing about 12.)
Only Itay is wrong.

steps.stem: The sum of three integers is divisible by 6. Which of the following statements is not necessarily true?
choices: When one of the numbers is divided by \(6\), the greatest possible remainder is \(5\).
If one of the numbers is divisible by \(6\), then the other two are too.
All three numbers can leave remainder \(4\) when divided by \(6\).
If two of the numbers are divisible by \(6\), then the third is too.
explanation: Think in remainders: the remainders of the three numbers must add up to a multiple of 6.
(1) True: dividing by 6, the remainder is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5.
(2) Not necessarily: \(12+5+7=24\). 12 is divisible by 6, but 5 and 7 are not.
(3) Possible: \(10+16+22=48\), and each number leaves remainder 4.
(4) True: two numbers leave 0 and the sum leaves 0, so the third leaves 0.

steps.stem: When a positive integer is divided by 9, the quotient is 7 and the remainder is 4. What is the integer?
explanation: Number \(=\) divisor \(\cdot\) quotient \(+\) remainder: \(9\cdot7+4=67\).

steps.stem: When the positive integer \(x\) is divided by 14, the remainder is 4. What will be the remainder if \(x\) is divided by 7?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
explanation: \(x=14k+4=7\cdot2k+4\). The part \(14k\) is made of full sevens.
So the remainder by 7 is 4. (7 divides 14, so the remainder carries over.)
Trap: \(7-4=3\) is a difference, not a remainder.

steps.stem: \(75\%\) of the employees of a certain company come to work by train. Which of the following could be the total number of employees in the company?
explanation: \(75\%=\frac34\). Build it from the inside: the company has \(4k\) employees, and \(3k\) of them come by train. So the total is divisible by 4.
So 412 (\(\frac34\cdot412=309\) come by train).

steps.stem: What will be the remainder if \(12{,}345\) is divided by 9?
explanation: Digit sum: \(1+2+3+4+5=15\), and 15 divided by 9 leaves 6.
A number leaves the same remainder by 9 as its digit sum, so the answer is 6.

steps.stem: What is the units digit of \(7^4\)?
explanation: Multiply only the units digits: \(7\cdot7=49\to9\), \(9\cdot7=63\to3\), \(3\cdot7=21\to1\).

steps.stem: How many odd numbers between 0 and 80 leave a remainder of 3 when divided by 5?
explanation: The numbers that leave 3: \(3, 8, 13, 18, \ldots, 78\). They go up by 5, so they alternate odd, even.
The odd ones end in 3: \(3, 13, 23, 33, 43, 53, 63, 73\). That is 8 numbers.
Trap: 16 counts all the numbers that leave 3, odd and even.

steps.stem: \(x\) is a positive integer. \(18+6x\) is not necessarily divisible by:
explanation: \(18+6x=6(3+x)\), so it is always divisible by 6, and therefore by 2 and by 3.
By 4? Try \(x=2\): \(18+12=30\), and 30 is not divisible by 4. So 4 is not necessarily a divisor.

steps.stem: When the positive integer \(x\) is divided by 8, the remainder is 5. What will be the remainder if \(3x\) is divided by 8?
explanation: Multiply the remainder: \(3\cdot5=15\), and 15 divided by 8 leaves 7.

steps.stem: A guide splits a group of hikers into teams of 4. Then she splits them into teams of 5. Each time, there is exactly one team with only 3 hikers. Which of the following could be the number of hikers in the group?
explanation: The number leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4 and when divided by 5.
Take away the remainder: \(n-3\) is divisible by 4 and by 5, so by 20.

steps.stem: Which of the following numbers is divisible by 11?
explanation: Alternate plus and minus: \(3-7+4=0\), so 374 is divisible by 11 (\(374=11\cdot34\)).

steps.stem: Which of the following numbers is divisible by 18?
explanation: \(18=2\cdot9\), and 2 and 9 have no common factor. (Not \(3\cdot6\): 3 and 6 share a 3.)
Check "even" and "digit sum is divisible by 9": \(2{,}346\): sum 15 ✗. \(5{,}445\): sum 18, but odd ✗. \(3{,}258\): even, sum 18 ✓. \(1{,}356\): sum 15 ✗.
Trap: \(2{,}346\) and \(1{,}356\) are divisible by 3 and by 6, but not by 18.

steps.stem: How many three-digit numbers are divisible by both 3 and 8?
explanation: 3 and 8 have no common factor, so the numbers are divisible by 24.
First: \(120=24\cdot5\) (\(96=24\cdot4\) has two digits). Last: \(984=24\cdot41\) (\(24\cdot42=1{,}008\) has four digits).

steps.stem: A grandmother has \(x\) stickers. She divides them equally among her 3 grandchildren. The eldest grandchild divides her share equally among 2 friends, and the second grandchild divides her share equally among 7 friends, with nothing left over. What is the smallest possible value of \(x\)?
explanation: Each grandchild gets \(\frac{x}{3}\) stickers. This share is divisible by 2 and by 7. They have no common factor, so it is divisible by 14.
So \(x=3\cdot14k=42k\). The smallest value is \(x=42\): each grandchild gets 14, and \(14\div2=7\), \(14\div7=2\) ✓.
14 and 21 fail: \(\frac{14}{3}\) is not a whole number, and \(\frac{21}{3}=7\) is not divisible by 2. 84 works, but it is not the smallest.

steps.stem: A coach has \(x\) balls. He tries to divide them equally among 5 teams, but 2 balls are left over. Then he decides that one team will get exactly twice as many balls as each of the other four teams. This time all the balls are given out. What is the smallest possible value of \(x\)?
explanation: First condition: \(x\) leaves remainder 2 when divided by 5.
Second condition: four teams get \(s\) balls each and the fifth gets \(2s\), so \(x=s+s+s+s+2s=6s\). \(x\) is divisible by 6.
Multiples of 6: \(6=5+1\) leaves 1 ✗; \(12=10+2\) leaves 2 ✓. So \(x=12\) (shares 2, 2, 2, 2 and 4).
42 also works, but it is not the smallest. 30 leaves 0, and 22 is not divisible by 6.

steps.stem:
Given:
\(\begin{cases} b=2a \\ c=2b \\ d=2c \end{cases}\)
(\(a\) is a positive integer). \(a+b+c+d\) is necessarily divisible by:
explanation: Write everything with \(a\): \(b=2a\), \(c=4a\), \(d=8a\).
\(a+b+c+d=a+2a+4a+8a=15a\), so it is always divisible by 15.
It is not necessarily divisible by 2, 4 or 8: for \(a=1\) the sum is 15.

steps.stem: A pizzeria's phone number has 7 identical digits (for example, 5555555). Its delivery line is the phone number plus 1. What will be the remainder if the sum of the digits of the delivery-line number is divided by 7?
explanation: Call the repeated digit \(d\).
If \(d\le8\), adding 1 changes only the last digit: the digits are \(d\) six times and then \(d+1\). Their sum is \(7d+1\), which leaves remainder 1.
If \(d=9\): \(9{,}999{,}999+1=10{,}000{,}000\). The digit sum is 1, so the remainder is 1 again.

steps.stem: When the positive integer \(a\) is divided by 9, the remainder is 2. What will be the remainder if \(a+1\) is divided by 6?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
explanation: 6 does not divide 9, so the remainder by 9 does not give the remainder by 6. Check with numbers.
Two different remainders, so it cannot be determined. (Trap: \(2+1=3\) keeps the old remainder.)
Method 2 · Tag it: \(a=9k+2\), so \(a+1=9k+3\). The tag \(9k\) is not always a multiple of \(6\) (\(9\), \(18\), \(27\), …), so the remainder by \(6\) moves.
\(k=0\) gives \(3\), remainder \(3\). \(k=1\) gives \(12\), remainder \(0\). So it cannot be determined (choice 4).

steps.stem: Given: \(y=17x+3\) (\(x\) is a positive integer), and \(y\) is divisible by 10. Which of the following could be the value of \(x\)?
explanation: \(y\) ends in 0, so \(17x\) ends in 7 (because \(7+3=10\)).
The units digit of \(17x\) depends only on \(7\cdot\)(the units digit of \(x\)). \(7\cdot1=7\) ends in 7, so \(x\) ends in 1.

steps.stem: \(n\) is a two-digit positive integer, and \(n^2-n\) is divisible by 10. What could be the units digit of \(n\)?
explanation: \(n^2-n=n(n-1)\): two numbers in a row, so it is always even.
For 10 it also needs a 5: \(n\) or \(n-1\) is divisible by 5. So \(n\) ends in 0 or 5, or \(n-1\) ends in 0 or 5 (\(n\) ends in 1 or 6).
Among the choices, only 0. Check: \(n=30\): \(900-30=870\) ✓. (Trap: 4 makes \(n+1\) a multiple of 5, but the expression has \(n-1\).)

steps.stem: Gil, Hila and Ido each have the same number \(N\) of toy bricks. Gil built 7 towers of equal height, using all his bricks. Hila built 2 towers whose heights differ by exactly 1, using all her bricks. Ido built 3 towers of different heights, using all his bricks, and his tallest tower has 9 bricks. What is the value of \(N\)?
explanation: Gil: \(N\) is divisible by 7. Hila: \(N=h+(h+1)=2h+1\), so \(N\) is odd. That leaves 21 and 35.
Ido: \(N=a+b+9\) with \(a<b<9\). The most is \(7+8+9=24\), so \(N\ne35\).
\(N=21\) works: for example, \(4+8+9=21\).

steps.stem: \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are integers, and \(x+y+z\) is divisible by 4. Which of the following statements is necessarily not correct?
choices: \(x\) and \(y\) each leave remainder \(1\) when divided by \(4\), and \(z\) leaves remainder \(2\).
\(x\) leaves remainder \(3\) when divided by \(4\), and \(y+z\) leaves remainder \(1\) when divided by \(4\).
\(x+y\) leaves remainder \(3\) when divided by \(4\), and \(z\) is divisible by \(4\).
explanation: Add the remainders. In (4): \(3+0=3\), so \(x+y+z\) would leave 3. That contradicts the given, so (4) is never correct.

steps.stem: \(n\) is a positive integer divisible by 3. What is the greatest number that necessarily divides \(n(n+3)\)?
explanation: \(k\) and \(k+1\) are two numbers in a row, so \(k(k+1)\) is even. Therefore \(n(n+3)\) is divisible by \(9\cdot2=18\).
Nothing bigger is certain: \(n=3\) gives \(3\cdot6=18\), which is not divisible by 27 or 36.

steps.stem: \(A\) is an even positive integer. Given: \(n=A^3+24A^2+80A\). \(n\) is necessarily divisible by:
explanation: One of \(m\), \(m+2\), \(m+10\) is divisible by 3: if \(m\) leaves 0, it is \(m\); if \(m\) leaves 1, then \(m+2\) leaves \(1+2=3\), that is 0; if \(m\) leaves 2, then \(m+10\) leaves \(2+10=12\), that is 0. So \(n\) is divisible by \(8\cdot3=24\).
Knock out the others with examples: \(A=2\) gives \(n=2\cdot6\cdot22=264\), which is not divisible by 16 or 48. \(A=4\) gives \(n=4\cdot8\cdot24=768\), which is not divisible by 132.
Trap: the smallest case (264) is not the answer. It only gives the biggest possible divisor.

steps.stem: Given: \(y=\frac{\sqrt2\cdot x}{3}\), and \(y\) is an integer divisible by 4. What is the greatest number that necessarily divides \(x^2\)?
explanation: Solve for \(x\): \(x=\frac{3y}{\sqrt2}\), so \(x^2=\frac{9y^2}{2}\).
Write \(y=4k\): \(x^2=\frac{9\cdot16k^2}{2}=72k^2\). So \(x^2\) is always divisible by 72.
Nothing bigger is certain: \(k=1\) gives \(x^2=72\).

steps.stem: Ron has 90 light bulbs, numbered 1 to 90, and all of them are off. In round 1 he turns on every bulb. In round 2 he changes the state of every second bulb (2, 4, 6, …): a bulb that is on is turned off, and a bulb that is off is turned on. In round 3 he changes the state of every third bulb, and so on, up to round 90 (in which he changes only bulb 90). Which of the following bulbs is on at the end?
explanation: Bulb \(k\) changes state once in every round \(d\) where \(d\) divides \(k\). So it changes state as many times as \(k\) has divisors.
It starts off, so it ends on only after an odd number of changes.
Divisors come in pairs (\(d\) and \(\frac{k}{d}\)), except when \(d\cdot d=k\). So only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors.
\(64=8^2\) (divisors 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64: seven changes, so it ends on). 50, 72 and 88 are not squares, so they end off.
